faq.q: What causes the most holiday stress?
faq.a: Money is the most common answer. In a 2023 Harris Poll of 2,061 U.S. adults for the American Psychological Association, 58% named spending or not having enough money, 40% finding the right gifts and 38% missing loved ones. In the American Psychiatric Association's 2025 poll of 2,203 adults, grief or missing someone came first at 48%, followed by gifts (46%), family dynamics (32%) and loneliness (31%).

faq.q: How do you deal with difficult family during the holidays?
faq.a: Plan for the moments you can predict with if-then plans, such as "If Mom comments on my plate, then I'll say I'm happy with it and ask about her garden." A 2006 meta-analysis of 94 tests found if-then plans helped people reach goals with a medium-to-large effect (d = 0.65). Have a few short lines ready, name your feeling silently when it hits, and step out for air if you need to.

faq.q: How do you set boundaries with family over the holidays?
faq.a: Frame each boundary as what you will do rather than what others must do. Set it early and keep it about time, topic or money, for example "We'll come for lunch and head out around four" or "One small gift per person this year." Say it once, kindly, and repeat the same sentence rather than re-explaining it.

faq.q: Why do I feel depressed after the holidays?
faq.a: A post-holiday dip is common. A 2011 review by Sansone and Sansone found psychiatric emergency visits, self-harm and suicide attempts tend to be lower around Christmas and rebound afterward. Planning something to look forward to in mid-January and checking in on people who had a hard season can help. If low mood lasts more than two weeks, talk to a doctor.

faq.q: How do you cope with grief during the holidays?
faq.a: Decide on purpose whether to keep, change or skip each tradition this year, make room for the person by saying their name or cooking their dish, and tell someone you may need to step away. Treat yourself with the kindness you'd give a friend. If grief feels as raw months later as it did at first, or you think about hurting yourself, get help; in the U.S. you can call or text 988.

informationGain: Instead of a generic tip list, it maps each driver of holiday stress in the latest APA and American Psychiatric Association polls (money, expectations, family friction, grief, loneliness, the January rebound) to the specific technique studies have tested for it, including a 1997 implementation-intention experiment run over Christmas, with sample sizes, effect sizes and limits, plus ready-to-use dinner-table scripts.
